title: Spring temperature adjustment reduced annual bloom agreement in three selected US lilac samples from 1965 to 2008
abstract: We tested how much local spring temperature explained annual bloom agreement between fixed nearby lilac sites. We used US legacy records from 1965 to 2008 and selected disjoint site pairs with at least 12 shared years. Separate site models removed a linear year trend, then added March-April temperature. Each year was left out of its own fit. Mean pair correlation fell from 0.683 to 0.509 in the early East, 0.565 to 0.341 in the early West, and 0.595 to 0.295 in the later East. The four-test adjusted bootstrap intervals for these reductions were above zero. The later West had one pair and an uncertain result. Summer adjustment changed agreement little. Spring adjustment also reduced held-out date error. Agreement remained after adjustment. These are weather associations in selected planted shrubs, not causal climate-change or pollution effects. Missing visit histories, different lilac types and bloom rules, short series, and invalid bootstrap draws limit inference. Primary intervals omit 1.18-14.05 percent of draws and are conditional on valid fits. Code, exact source hashes, derived data, all valid draws, checks, and a figure are included.

display.caption: Mean annual agreement in bloom timing at fixed lilac site pairs before and after local weather adjustment. Left: held-out-year residual correlations and pointwise 95% block bootstrap intervals. Right: spring correlation reductions and 98.75% intervals for four primary tests. Intervals are conditional on fixed selected pairs and valid bootstrap draws. The later West has one pair.
